newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Employment watch begins.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Employment watch begins.

text.p: Without any major economic releases to grab its attention on Friday, the U.S. credit market will begin looking ahead to its most cherished of indicators -- the non-farm payrolls report.

The September jobs data will not hit the tape for another week, but market participants are already hoping the report will lend additional support to the Federal Reserve's steady rate decision and allow Treasuries to add to recent gains.
"People will be looking forward at the calendar for the following week and the fixation will be on employment," said Russell Sheldon, senior economist at Mellon Bank.
"You won't get anything new but I think the market chatter will be revolving around the fact that economists are calling for a softer looking report," he added.

Economists said the the market has already begun talking about a reassuring headline figure well below the 200,000 mark, mainly a result of an expected decline in teacher employment. The unemployment rate is seen rising and wage numbers are forecast on the favorable side as well.
"That's giving a nice buzz to the market," said Cary Leahey, senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities, referring to jobs report estimates.
"I don't see anything that's going to get in the way of the market," he added.

Friday's data -- the final revision to second quarter Gross Domestic Product and the University of Michigan's final sentiment index for September -- should have little impact on the market, analysts predicted.

Economists surveyed by Reuters are calling for a 4.6 percent GDP growth rate for the second quarter versus a 4.8 percent reading in the second estimate. They expect the price index and implicit price deflator to remain unchanged from the respective 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent levels reported previously.
The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index is expected to register 95.1 for September, down from the previous month's 95.3 reading, but still relatively robust.

"Sentiment will continue to look positive but people have already seen the Conference Board's numbers so they are unlikely to panic at the University of Michigan figures," said Mellon's Sheldon, referring to strong confidence numbers released earlier this week.
As trading winds down on Friday, minutes from the August 20 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting will also garner some attention, economists said.
Of particular interest to the market would be any hints of further division among Fed policymakers after Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern's dissent at the July meeting.
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond was up 19/32 at 98-11/32 to yield 6.88 percent in late trading on Thursday. The federal funds rate is expected to open around 5-1/4 percent. -- 212 859-1673
